Hackers exploit critical Atlassian flaw after public PoC release

Attackers began probing the critical unauthenticated Atlassian file-access flaw CVE-2026-21589 within hours of a public proof of concept, potentially enabling Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket compromise through exposed Crowd credentials. Organizations running affected self-hosted Atlassian products should patch immediately or apply mitigations to restrict access and block traversal patterns.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-21589 is a critical unauthenticated file-access flaw affecting self-hosted Atlassian products including Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye, and Jira Service Management Data Center.
  • 02Previdian observed attempts to exploit CVE-2026-21589 on its honeypot network within two hours of watchTowr publishing technical research and a public proof of concept.
  • 03The flaw involves a shared web-resource library converting double colons into forward slashes, which can enable directory-traversal requests through plugin resource endpoints to retrieve protected application files.
  • 04In certain Crowd-integrated Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket deployments, attackers may be able to read credentials from crowd.properties and use Crowd’s API to create administrator accounts.
  • 05Atlassian recommends installing security updates as soon as possible or applying mitigations such as restricting external access and blocking specified traversal patterns.

A critical unauthenticated file-access flaw, CVE-2026-21589, affecting self-hosted Atlassian products is being exploited shortly after public technical details and a proof of concept were released. Previdian detected exploitation attempts on its honeypot network within two hours of watchTowr publishing its research. The affected products include Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. A Nuclei template has also been released to automate scans for vulnerable systems.

The flaw stems from a shared web-resource library converting double colons into forward slashes, enabling directory-traversal requests through plugin resource endpoints to read protected files in an application’s web root without authentication. watchTowr confirmed file reads in Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket, although its technique could not traverse outside the Tomcat application context. In certain Crowd-integrated deployments, attackers could read plaintext credentials from the crowd.properties file and use Crowd’s API to create a Jira administrator account. The article notes that restricting Crowd access to allowed IP addresses can make this escalation significantly more difficult.

Atlassian urged administrators to apply available security updates as soon as possible, while noting it cannot determine whether individual customer instances were compromised. Recommended mitigations include restricting external network access, using WAF or proxy rules to block specified traversal patterns, and applying product-specific rewrite rules. Previdian expects attempts to increase due to the public proof of concept, automated scanning support, and the broad set of affected products.

  • Although watchTowr’s file-reading technique could not move outside the Tomcat application context, it could still lead to administrator access by exposing Crowd credentials stored within affected applications.
  • Restricting which IP addresses can reach Crowd can significantly complicate administrator-account creation, because an attacker would otherwise need to reach Crowd directly or use another system to do so.
  • A publicly released Nuclei template makes it easier to automatically scan for exposed vulnerable systems, increasing the practical risk soon after the proof of concept was published.
  • Atlassian’s mitigation options differ by product, with Tomcat RewriteValve rules recommended for Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira, Bamboo, and Crowd, and a URL rewrite rule recommended for Bitbucket.

Hackers began testing a serious flaw in self-hosted Atlassian software just hours after researchers published instructions showing how it could be abused. The problem affects products such as Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket, and may let an outsider read protected files without signing in. In some setups, those files can contain account details that could let an attacker create an administrator account, giving them broad control over the affected system. Organizations using these products need to install the available fixes or limit outside access because automated tools now make it easier to find vulnerable systems.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a critical, actively exploited unauthenticated flaw affecting widely used self-hosted Atlassian products, with public proof-of-concept code and automated scanning support already available. In some Crowd-integrated deployments, exploitation can expose credentials that enable attackers to create administrator accounts.

Ransomware has a new target. Is your backup ready?

Ransomware operators increasingly target backup infrastructure first, deleting or encrypting recovery data to force victims into paying. Organizations need immutable, isolated backups with separate credentials, timely patching, and regularly tested restores to preserve recovery options.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Ransomware groups are increasingly targeting backup infrastructure by deleting, reformatting, or encrypting recovery data before encrypting other systems.
  • 02The article cites ALPHV/BlackCat’s 2024 Change Healthcare intrusion, BlackMatter’s 2021 attacks on NEW Cooperative and Crystal Valley, and a Gunra case in which primary and disaster-recovery backup data were deleted.
  • 03Shared networks and administrator credentials can allow a single compromised account to reach both production systems and backup environments.
  • 04The article recommends immutable backup storage, separate network and credential access, prompt patching of backup software, and regular restore testing.
  • 05IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the average cost of a ransomware incident at $5.08 million, according to the article.

Ransomware groups are increasingly targeting backup systems to remove victims’ ability to restore data without paying. The article cites ALPHV/BlackCat’s 2024 intrusion at Change Healthcare, where inadequate backup isolation contributed to prolonged recovery, as well as BlackMatter attacks that used compromised administrator credentials to locate and wipe backup stores. It also describes a Gunra case in which stolen credentials reportedly enabled deletion of backup and archived data at both a primary data center and a disaster-recovery site.

The article argues that multiple backup copies are not sufficient if they share networks, administrative accounts, or other access paths with production systems. It recommends immutable write-once storage, separate network and credential access, multi-factor authentication, role-based access controls, prompt patching of backup software, and regular restore testing. It cites IBM’s estimate of an average $5.08 million cost for ransomware incidents and notes that backup loss can add operational disruption and reputational damage. The article also says organizations often understand these protections but lack the budget, trained staff, and operational capacity to implement them.

  • Having backups in both a primary data center and a disaster-recovery site may not provide protection if both environments can be accessed with the same stolen credentials.
  • Backup servers may be especially exposed because organizations often patch them later than production systems and apply less monitoring, logging, and access control to them.
  • Immutable, write-once storage is presented as a baseline control because it can prevent even an administrator account from changing or deleting backup copies.
  • The article identifies resource constraints—not merely lack of awareness—as a major reason organizations fail to implement stronger backup protections.

The article warns that ransomware gangs are increasingly destroying or locking up an organization’s backup copies before locking its main systems, leaving victims with fewer ways to recover without paying. Recent examples include Change Healthcare, farm cooperatives in Iowa and Minnesota, and an unnamed organization whose main and emergency recovery sites were both reached with stolen account details. This can turn a disruption into a costly business crisis, with lost operations, major recovery costs, and damage to customer trust. Keeping backup copies separate, protected from deletion, and regularly tested can give organizations a way to recover even after an attacker gets into their network.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a sponsored, evergreen best-practice article about protecting backups from ransomware, supported by past examples rather than a newly reported incident or urgent technical finding. Its recommendations are relevant, but it does not provide actionable new intelligence about an active threat or specific patch.

Microsoft Outlook to block MSIX attachments starting November

Microsoft will block .msix and .msixbundle email attachments by default in Outlook on the web and the new Outlook for Windows beginning in early November, with full rollout expected by mid-November. Administrators can allow these package types through OWA mailbox policies if their organization requires them.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft will add .msix and .msixbundle files to the default blocked attachment list for Outlook on the web and the new Outlook for Windows.
  • 02The change will begin rolling out to Exchange Online users in early November and is expected to reach general availability by mid-November.
  • 03Once the policy update is applied, users will be unable to send, receive, open, or download .msix and .msixbundle attachments in the affected Outlook clients.
  • 04Administrators can allow these file types if needed by adding them to the AllowedFileTypes property of users' OwaMailboxPolicy objects.
  • 05Microsoft said the update is intended to strengthen protection against potentially unsafe attachments and follows earlier Outlook restrictions on .library-ms, .search-ms, and inline SVG images.

Microsoft will add .msix and .msixbundle files to Outlook’s blocked-attachment list for Outlook on the web and the new Outlook for Windows. The rollout for Exchange Online users is scheduled to begin in early November and reach general availability by mid-November. Once applied, users will not be able to send, receive, open, or download these attachment types in the affected clients.

MSIX files are Windows application installation packages tailored to particular computer architectures or configurations, while MSIX bundles package multiple MSIX files for use across architectures. Microsoft will add the file types to the BlockedFileTypes list in both default and custom OWA mailbox policies. Organizations that need to use them can allow them by adding the extensions to the AllowedFileTypes property of users’ OwaMailboxPolicy objects.

Microsoft said most organizations are not expected to be affected because the file types are infrequently used. The company described the move as part of ongoing efforts to protect organizations from potentially unsafe attachments and to limit features abused in phishing and malicious-software campaigns. Previous Outlook restrictions covered .library-ms and .search-ms files, as well as risky inline SVG images.

  • The block will be applied not only to Microsoft’s default Outlook web mailbox policy but also to any custom OWA mailbox policies created in a tenant, so organizations using customized policies are included in the change.
  • Organizations that legitimately use these Windows installation packages have a documented exception path: administrators can add .msix and .msixbundle to the AllowedFileTypes setting in the relevant mailbox policy.
  • The restriction affects the complete attachment lifecycle in Outlook on the web and new Outlook for Windows, preventing users from sending, receiving, opening, or downloading the files rather than only blocking one action.
  • Microsoft frames the change as part of a continuing effort to remove or limit Outlook and Windows features that have been abused in phishing and malicious-software campaigns, following blocks on .library-ms, .search-ms, and risky inline SVG images.

Microsoft will soon block two types of Windows app-installation files, called .msix and .msixbundle, from being sent or opened as attachments in Outlook on the web and the new Outlook for Windows. This affects Exchange Online users, although most organizations are not expected to use these file types often; organizations that need them can ask their administrators to allow them. The change is meant to reduce the chance that unsafe email attachments are used to harm organizations, as Microsoft continues restricting file types that have been misused in phishing and malicious-software campaigns.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete, upcoming Microsoft security-control change affecting Exchange Online users of Outlook on the web and the new Outlook for Windows. Security and messaging administrators should assess whether their organizations use MSIX attachments and prepare an exception through OWA mailbox policies if necessary.

SonicWall warns of max severity SSRF flaw in SMA1000 gateways

SonicWall released hotfixes for CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity unauthenticated SSRF flaw in SMA1000 appliances that could let remote attackers access internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations. The flaw is not currently known to be exploited, but organizations should patch promptly given recent attacks on SMA1000 gateways.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SonicWall released hotfixes for CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity server-side request forgery flaw in the Appliance WorkPlace interface of SMA1000 6210, 7210, and 8200v appliances.
  • 02A remote attacker without authentication could potentially abuse the flaw to make an affected appliance issue requests on their behalf, reach internal functions, and perform unauthorized operations.
  • 03SonicWall said there is currently no evidence that CVE-2026-102255 or the other issues addressed in the release are being exploited in the wild.
  • 04The flaw does not affect the SMA 100 Series product line or SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls.
  • 05Shadowserver tracks more than 400 Internet-exposed SMA1000 appliances, although some may already have been patched.

SonicWall has released hotfixes for CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity server-side request forgery flaw affecting the Appliance WorkPlace interface in SMA1000 6210, 7210, and 8200v appliances. The flaw is an unintended alternate access path that a remote attacker without privileges could use with low complexity. An attacker could potentially cause an affected appliance to send requests on their behalf, reach internal functions, and perform unauthorized operations.

SonicWall said it has no evidence that the issues addressed by the release are being exploited in the wild and urged SMA1000 customers to upgrade to the fixed version. The issue does not affect the SMA 100 Series or SSL-VPN services running on SonicWall firewalls, while Shadowserver tracks more than 400 internet-exposed SMA1000 appliances. The warning is significant because several SMA1000 zero-days have been exploited this year to install Sou5, OrangeTail, and RootRun malware, with CISA linking some of those attacks to ransomware gangs.

  • The affected SMA1000 systems are enterprise remote-access gateways used by government agencies, managed service providers, and large corporations, so a flaw in them can provide a path toward internal organizational functions.
  • More than 400 SMA1000 appliances are currently visible on the internet according to Shadowserver, creating a substantial pool of systems that may need the hotfix.
  • Recent SMA1000 zero-day flaws were used for weeks to install Sou5, OrangeTail, and RootRun malware, and CISA linked those attacks to ransomware gangs, making prompt patching particularly important even though this newer flaw has not been observed in use.
  • CISA has added 19 SonicWall vulnerabilities to its actively exploited catalog over the past four years, including 13 that were also used in ransomware attacks.

SonicWall released emergency fixes for a serious weakness in its SMA1000 remote-access devices, which are used by organizations to let people connect to internal apps and networks from outside. The issue could allow an outsider with no account to make the device contact internal parts of an organization and carry out actions they should not be allowed to perform. It affects certain SMA1000 models, not SonicWall’s SMA 100 products or the remote-access feature on its firewalls. Although SonicWall has not seen this specific problem used in attacks yet, similar flaws in these devices have recently been used to install harmful software and have been linked to ransomware groups.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

SonicWall released hotfixes for a maximum-severity unauthenticated flaw in SMA1000 remote-access gateways that could enable unauthorized internal operations. While not known to be exploited, the affected appliances are internet-exposed and have been repeatedly targeted in recent zero-day and ransomware-linked campaigns.

Hackers hijack Google domains after breaching ccTLD registries

Attackers compromised ccTLD registry operators for Ghana, Sierra Leone, and American Samoa to alter DNS records, obtain fraudulent HTTPS certificates, and hijack domains including Google properties. Google blocked known malicious certificates in Chrome but warned that affected domains may remain unrecognized and non-Chrome users may not be protected.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers compromised third-party operators of the .GH, .SL, and .AS country-code domain registries and modified authoritative DNS records for affected domains.
  • 02The DNS changes enabled the attackers to obtain unauthorized HTTPS certificates and redirect affected domains, including several Google domains, to infrastructure they controlled.
  • 03Google said its own systems were not compromised and that it blocked known unauthorized certificates in Chrome using CRLSets while working with issuing certificate authorities to revoke them.
  • 04Certificate Transparency logs revealed additional potentially affected organizations, including global brands and widely used online services, prompting Google to block more related certificates in Chrome.
  • 05Google warned that it may not have identified every affected domain and that its Chrome-focused protections do not reliably protect users of other browsers.

Attackers compromised third-party operators of the .GH, .SL, and .AS country-code domain registries and changed authoritative DNS records for affected domains. The incident included several Google domains, though Google said its own systems were not compromised. By controlling DNS records, the attackers could redirect domains to infrastructure they controlled and obtain unauthorized HTTPS certificates.

The fraudulent certificates could allow the attackers to impersonate legitimate brands and serve arbitrary content to visitors. Google blocked known unauthorized and related certificates in Chrome through CRLSets, coordinated revocations with issuing certificate authorities, and used Certificate Transparency logs to find additional potentially affected organizations. Google cautioned that it may not have identified every impacted domain and that Chrome’s protections do not reliably cover users of other browsers.

Google advised domain owners to monitor Certificate Transparency logs across their full domain portfolios, including parked domains, and to publish restrictive CAA records. CAA records cannot stop certificate issuance during an active DNS hijack, but Google said they can limit further certificates obtained through cached domain validation after legitimate DNS control is restored. The company did not identify the attackers or state how many certificates were confirmed to have been hijacked.

  • Control of authoritative DNS records can let an attacker satisfy certificate ownership checks and obtain valid HTTPS certificates without compromising the targeted company’s own systems.
  • Certificate Transparency logs helped Google identify additional suspected victims after its initial response, showing that public certificate records can support incident discovery beyond the first known affected domains.
  • CAA records cannot prevent certificate issuance while DNS control is actively hijacked, but Google says they can limit additional certificates obtained through cached validation after legitimate DNS control is restored.
  • Chrome’s CRLSet mechanism can rapidly block selected certificates for Chrome users, but this protection does not reliably extend to people using other browsers.

Attackers broke into organizations that manage internet addresses for Ghana, Sierra Leone, and American Samoa, then redirected some website addresses—including several Google domains—to their own servers. This allowed them to obtain valid-looking security credentials and potentially show visitors fake content while appearing to be legitimate brands. Google blocked known fraudulent credentials in Chrome, but says it may not have found every affected website and people using other browsers may not receive the same protection.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete DNS registry compromise that enabled unauthorized HTTPS certificates and domain hijacking for Google properties and other major organizations. It has broad relevance because the attack can bypass normal website ownership checks without compromising the targeted organization’s own systems, and protections may not cover all browsers or affected domains.

Ransomware recovery CEO charged over secret ransom payments

MonsterCloud owner Zohar Pinhasi has been charged with wire-fraud offenses for allegedly secretly paying ransomware gangs for decryption keys while claiming the company used proprietary recovery technology. Prosecutors say the firm facilitated more than $8 million in ransoms and charged victims over $19 million for remediation services.
KEY POINTS
  • 01MonsterCloud owner Zohar Pinhasi was charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud over an alleged ransomware-decryption scheme that prosecutors say operated from June 2018 through June 2023.
  • 02Prosecutors allege that MonsterCloud claimed it could recover encrypted customer data using proprietary technology, but instead commonly contacted ransomware operators and paid them for decryption keys.
  • 03The indictment alleges that MonsterCloud charged clients substantially more than the ransoms it paid, including one case involving an approximately $8,200 payment to a ransomware gang and a roughly $150,000 charge to the victim.
  • 04Prosecutors say Pinhasi and co-conspirators facilitated more than $8 million in ransom payments while charging hundreds of U.S. and Canadian companies more than $19 million for recovery and remediation services.
  • 05Pinhasi pleaded not guilty after surrendering and was released on a $2 million bond, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

Zohar Pinhasi, owner of Florida-based ransomware remediation company MonsterCloud, was indicted in the Eastern District of New York on charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that from June 2018 through June 2023, he misled customers by claiming MonsterCloud could recover encrypted data using proprietary technology without paying the criminals responsible. Pinhasi surrendered, pleaded not guilty, and was released on a $2 million bond; he faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

According to the indictment, MonsterCloud allegedly obtained decryption keys by contacting ransomware operators and paying them, often as its first step rather than only after other recovery efforts failed. Prosecutors say the company then used decrypted files supplied through those payments as proof that it could restore customer data, while charging customers far more than the ransom amounts. The alleged operation facilitated more than \(8 million in ransom payments and charged hundreds of companies in the United States and Canada more than \)19 million for recovery and remediation services.

  • Although some MonsterCloud contracts disclosed that it might communicate with or pay cybercriminals, prosecutors allege the contracts represented this as a fallback after other recovery methods had failed rather than the usual first step.
  • The indictment alleges that decrypted sample files presented as proof of MonsterCloud’s recovery capability were supplied by the ransomware operations after payment, which could make paid decryption appear to be an independent technical solution.
  • A 2019 ProPublica investigation described a test in which researchers posing as ransomware victims received payment offers at attacker-controlled email accounts, which they traced to recovery firms including MonsterCloud.
  • The cited customer charges show that the alleged markup was not uniform: prosecutors describe one case rising from about $8,200 to $150,000 and another from about $236,000 to $380,000.

The owner of MonsterCloud, a company hired to help organizations recover files locked by criminals, has been charged with allegedly misleading customers about how it restored their data. Prosecutors say the company often paid the criminals for the unlock code, then charged victims much more while suggesting it used its own special recovery methods. Hundreds of companies in the United States and Canada may have paid for these services, showing that people hit by digital extortion can face further harm from businesses they trust to help them recover.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific federal fraud case with broad relevance for organizations selecting ransomware recovery providers. It highlights allegations that a remediation firm concealed ransom payments and significantly marked up recovery charges, but it does not describe an active technical threat or urgent patching need.

PoeLLM malware infects exposed AI servers in cryptomining attacks

PoeLLM cryptomining malware has compromised more than 3,400 exposed AI and developer-service servers, using infected hosts to scan for and exploit additional targets. It covertly derives its command-and-control address from a GitHub-hosted poem and targets services including LiteLLM and Gotenberg.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Black Lotus Labs reports that the PoeLLM cryptomining malware has compromised more than 3,400 servers, with up to 800 infected systems active on a single day.
  • 02PoeLLM targets exposed services including LiteLLM, Ollama, Gotenberg, and Gitea, and it can turn compromised servers into systems that scan for and attempt to infect additional targets.
  • 03The malware retrieves words or phrases from a poem hosted in a GitHub repository and converts them through a hard-coded dictionary into an IPv4 command-and-control address.
  • 04PoeLLM scans ports 3000 and 4000 associated with Gotenberg and LiteLLM and attempts to exploit CVE-2026-42271, which researchers said can be chained with CVE-2026-48710 for unauthenticated remote code execution.
  • 05Researchers observed victim communications with the Russian crypto-mining service Kryptex and assessed with moderate confidence that the operator may be Italian.

Black Lotus Labs reports that the PoeLLM cryptomining malware has compromised more than 3,400 servers, with as many as 800 infected systems active on a single day. The campaign has been active since at least April and has targeted systems in the United States and Western Europe. Many affected systems run exposed AI-related services such as LiteLLM and Ollama, as well as Gotenberg and Gitea.

PoeLLM is an ELF file named libgcrypt that retrieves words or phrases from a poem in a GitHub-hosted file and converts them into an IPv4 address for its command server. The malware includes remote-shell access, XMRig and Iron cryptocurrency miners, web scanning, and exploit-deployment capabilities. Infected servers scan ports associated with Gotenberg and LiteLLM and attempt to exploit CVE-2026-42271, which Horizon3.ai researchers said can be chained with CVE-2026-48710 for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Researchers found signs that several command servers used vulnerable router administration interfaces, suggesting reused compromised routers may support the operation. Black Lotus Labs could not confidently identify the operator but assessed with moderate confidence that the operator is Italian, based on malware comments and an Italy-based server hosting an administrative interface. Administrators are advised to apply updates, limit public exposure and access to trusted IPs, and check network logs for the published indicators of compromise.

  • PoeLLM can change its command-and-control destination without updating the malware by changing the words in a poem hosted on GitHub; researchers observed 11 such poem modifications.
  • Compromised servers are used not only for cryptocurrency mining but also as launchpads that scan ports 3000 and 4000 and attempt to spread to additional Gotenberg and LiteLLM systems.

Least Privilege for AI Agents: A Practical Guide for Security Leaders

AI agents should receive unique, task-specific, time-limited permissions rather than inheriting broad user or shared service-account access, because excessive access can turn prompt injection or mistakes into major data exposure. Effective controls combine agent identity and ownership, runtime enforcement, approval for high-impact actions, and continuous access review.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Least privilege for AI agents means giving each agent its own identity and only the tools and data access needed for a specific task, with access ending when the task is complete.
  • 02AI agents can inherit excessive user permissions or use shared service accounts, allowing them to reach data and systems they were not intended to access.
  • 03OWASP identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as root causes of excessive agency in AI systems.
  • 04Organizations should enforce controls while agents run, compare requested tasks with the data and tools an agent attempts to use, and require human approval for high-impact actions such as deleting data, changing permissions, or exporting sensitive records.
  • 05The article recommends discovering all approved and unsanctioned agents, mapping the data each identity can access, removing stale permissions, and regularly testing whether agent access can be revoked quickly.

AI agents need least-privilege access because their inherited permissions, shared service accounts, and ability to act at machine speed can expose far more data and systems than a task requires. The article defines this approach as assigning each agent a distinct identity, granting only task-specific access, making permissions expire when the task ends, and applying checks to high-impact actions. It notes that only 44% of organizations in a SailPoint survey reported having policies to secure agents, while 80% said their agents had taken unintended actions.

The article identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as root causes of excessive agency, echoing OWASP guidance. It recommends discovering all agents, mapping the data each identity can reach, removing stale permissions, using read-only and per-tool access by default, and requiring approval for actions such as deleting data, changing permissions, or exporting sensitive records. Runtime enforcement can compare an agent’s requested task with the data and tools it attempts to access, helping detect scope creep and enabling actions such as alerting, blocking, modifying, logging, quarantining, or routing an action for human approval.

  • For an AI agent, access to sensitive data is as important as access to tools, because an agent can expose or act on information it can reach even when it was not designed to use that information.
  • Prompt injection can effectively give an attacker the permissions of the person whose account an agent is using; Varonis' SearchLeak research described this risk for Copilot Enterprise operating with a user's full graph permissions.
  • Runtime checks can identify scope creep by comparing an agent's stated task with its actual behavior, such as a customer-account summarization request leading the agent to retrieve records for many more accounts.
  • A named human owner is necessary for each agent because agents themselves cannot be accountable for the actions they take.
  • Access reviews must be continuous rather than one-time because agent tools, data connections, and models can change frequently, causing permissions to drift out of date.

The article explains why AI helpers at work should only be allowed to see data and perform actions needed for one specific job, and only for as long as that job lasts. Companies are affected because these helpers can inherit broad employee or shared account access, which can let them accidentally expose HR, financial, customer, or legal records. If someone tricks an AI helper with a malicious instruction, that person may gain access to whatever the helper can reach, so companies need clear ownership, regular access reviews, and human approval for major actions such as deleting data or changing permissions.

Picus argues that agentic pentesting provides strong live proof of exploitability and attack paths but is too slow and limited in coverage to validate an enterprise continuously on its own.   • 04The article argues that agentic pentesting alone may cover only 20 to 30% of real exploitability in a typical enterprise, particularly because many CVEs have no working exploit.
  • 05Picus advocates combining exploitability validation, security control validation, and agentic pentesting in a shared findings model so that changes and exposures can be assessed within hours.

Picus argues that agentic pentesting can provide strong evidence by safely executing exploits to confirm individual exposures and by demonstrating chained routes from initial access to critical assets. The article says this proof is limited to systems the testing can reach and safely assess. It frames the central challenge as not only whether an exposure is exploitable, but also how quickly evidence is produced and how much of an organization’s environment is covered.

The article cites an eight-hour mean disclosure-to-exploitation time in 2026 and argues that annual, weekly, or weeks-long testing cycles leave major gaps. It says live exploitation may be unsuitable for critical production systems, large segments, and restricted or air-gapped areas, and that many CVEs lack a working exploit. Picus advocates combining agentic pentesting with exploitability validation and security-control validation in a shared findings model, using the type of change—such as a new CVE, observed campaign, or infrastructure change—to select the fastest and safest validation method.

  • It highlights a counterintuitive limitation of exploit-based testing: it is least useful immediately after a vulnerability is disclosed, when no working exploit may yet exist and rapid decisions are most needed.
  • The article argues that adding multiple autonomous pentesting tools does not resolve coverage limitations because tools using the same live-exploitation method share the same safety, access, and exploit-availability constraints.
  • It recommends selecting the validation approach based on the triggering change: broad exploitability checks for newly discovered flaws, defensive-control checks for campaigns or control changes, and live chained testing for infrastructure changes.
  • The article warns that separate tools and queues can recreate the duplicate and conflicting findings problems seen in vulnerability management, making a shared evidence-backed findings model operationally important.

The article says automated, AI-driven security testing can show whether a real weakness can be used to break into a company’s systems and move toward important data or services. However, testing every system this way can take weeks and cannot safely be done on many critical, restricted, or disconnected systems, while criminals may begin using newly revealed flaws within hours. Picus argues that large organizations should combine this deeper testing with faster, safer checks across all affected systems so they can find and confirm problems soon after changes occur.

Unpatched Critical LMCache Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code Remotely

LMCache versions 0.3.9 through 0.5.5 contain an unpatched critical flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution when its multiprocess ZeroMQ server is exposed on a routable network address. Operators should keep the service bound to localhost or a trusted internal network, as no fixed release is available.
KEY POINTS
  • 01LMCache versions 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, along with 0.5.6 release candidates and the development branch, are affected by CVE-2026-105192, an unpatched critical remote code execution flaw.
  • 02The flaw affects LMCache multiprocess deployments whose ZeroMQ cache server is bound to a routable address, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to send a crafted message that executes code.
  • 03LMCache uses Python pickle to unpack one type of network message before validating its type, enabling malicious data to run code with the permissions of the LMCache process.
  • 04LMCache’s official container images run the LMCache process as root, according to JFrog, increasing the potential impact of successful exploitation.
  • 05Until a patched release is available, JFrog recommends keeping the LMCache multiprocess server on localhost or a trusted cluster network; firewall restrictions reduce but do not eliminate the risk.

A critical, unpatched flaw in LMCache can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on an LMCache cache server in multiprocess deployments. JFrog disclosed the issue as CVE-2026-105192 and rated it 9.8 when the server is exposed on a routable network address. The affected versions span LMCache 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, as well as 0.5.6 release candidates and the development branch.

The multiprocess server uses ZeroMQ for worker communication and accepts a message type that is decoded with Python pickle before its type is validated. A crafted network message can therefore execute commands with the permissions of the LMCache process, which JFrog says runs as root in the project’s official container images. The server is local-only by default, but it becomes reachable from other machines when configured with a routable address; LMCache’s Kubernetes example listens on all network interfaces.

No patched LMCache version is available, and JFrog recommends keeping the multiprocess server bound to localhost or a trusted cluster network. Firewall restrictions reduce exposure but do not prevent code execution by any host that is still allowed to connect. The article also notes unconfirmed additional LMCache reports and a separate vLLM denial-of-service issue, CVE-2026-105756, that was fixed in vLLM 0.30.0 and does not allow code execution.

  • The vulnerability is not remotely reachable in LMCache’s default configuration because the multiprocess server listens only on the local machine, but the project’s own Kubernetes example binds it to every network interface.
  • Restricting the port with a firewall lowers exposure but does not fully mitigate the issue, because any system still permitted to connect can execute code on the LMCache server.
  • Operators have no vendor-provided method to determine whether an LMCache server was already compromised, according to JFrog’s advisory.
  • The related vLLM flaw is distinct from the LMCache code-execution issue: it could crash affected deployments using the multiprocess connector but was fixed in vLLM 0.30.0 and does not permit code execution.
  • Six additional LMCache security reports were filed by one GitHub account, but they remain unconfirmed by maintainers and have no assigned CVEs or fixes.

Researchers found a serious weakness in LMCache, software used to help AI systems respond faster, that can let an outsider take control of a cache server without a password. The risk affects organizations that run LMCache in its multi-process setup and make the server reachable from other machines, including the project’s example setup for Kubernetes. There is no fix yet, and the attacker’s commands can run with the same permissions as LMCache—root-level control in the project’s official containers—so affected operators should keep it limited to the local machine or a trusted internal network.

This is a specific, unpatched critical remote code execution finding affecting LMCache multiprocess deployments, with potential root-level command execution in official containers when the service is network-accessible. It is especially important for organizations running LMCache with vLLM or Kubernetes, though the default localhost binding limits broader immediate exposure.

Cybersecurity researchers at CloudSEK and Checkmarx identified a long-running npm supply-chain campaign named MALFEX that distributes information stealers and remote-access tools to compromised Windows systems. The suspected lone operator has published 12 npm packages since August 2023, with eight identified as malicious. Those eight packages were downloaded 40,767 times in total, including 37,419 downloads of the still-live function-flag package.

The packages use installation-time scripts to deliver one of three payload paths: a loader for the Go-based Overlord RAT, the movinlike Node.js stealer, or a downloader. The movinlike stealer targets Discord, browsers, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallets, while three packages—tlxbnhd, tldriver, and mxdriver—download and run an Overlord executable. In function-flag version 1.7.3, a hidden routine triggered through its ASCII-art feature downloads node.exe from a remote host, saves it to %APPDATA%\node.exe, and runs it with a hidden window.

  • Each version of function-flag was found to retrieve its payload from a different location, which can complicate efforts to block a single download source.
  • In version 1.7.3, calling the package's ASCII-art feature with the "Bloody" font triggers the hidden download-and-execution routine.
  • Although researchers found Portuguese-language clues and Brazilian-associated account details, they explicitly cautioned that these clues indicate the operator's linguistic context rather than the campaign's target country.

Researchers found eight harmful software packages in npm, a widely used code-sharing service, that were downloaded more than 40,000 times. People who installed them on Windows could unknowingly receive tools that let criminals remotely control their computer or steal data from web browsers, Discord, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallets. This matters because developers and organizations may trust seemingly useful shared code, allowing a single bad download to expose personal accounts, money, and sensitive information.

KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers compromised the .gh, .sl, and .as country-code domain registries and changed authoritative DNS records, enabling them to obtain unauthorized HTTPS certificates for Google and YouTube domain names.

Attackers compromised the registries for the .gh, .sl, and .as country-code domains and changed authoritative DNS records, allowing them to obtain unauthorized HTTPS certificates for Google and YouTube domain names. Google said its own systems were not breached, but the incident put any domain under those endings at risk. Such certificates could allow an attacker to impersonate a legitimate encrypted website and read private information submitted by visitors.

Certificate Transparency logs showed at least 12 domain-validated certificates for seven Google and YouTube domains, logged from September 22 through September 27; Let’s Encrypt issued 11 and ZeroSSL issued one. Google blocked known unauthorized certificates in Chrome through CRLSets and worked with the issuing certificate authorities to revoke them, although it warned that protections may not extend reliably to other browsers and apps. Google advised domain owners to monitor certificate logs, use strict CAA records after regaining DNS control, and report unrequested certificates to the issuing certificate authority.

  • A DNS takeover can let an attacker pass a certificate authority’s normal proof-of-domain-control check without the certificate authority necessarily doing anything wrong.
  • The known certificates remained active from roughly a day and a half to nearly a week before revocation, and a certificate for .as was logged after the .gh certificates had already been revoked.
  • CAA records cannot prevent certificate issuance during an active DNS hijack because an attacker controlling DNS can alter them, but strict records can block additional certificates requested later using a previously completed domain check.
  • Certificate authorities may reuse a completed domain-control check for up to 200 days under current rules, making post-incident DNS recovery and restrictive CAA records important.

Attackers took control of parts of the systems that direct internet traffic for the .gh, .sl, and .as web-address endings, then obtained security certificates for some Google and YouTube addresses. Those certificates could have let them create convincing fake encrypted websites and read information that visitors thought they were sending safely to the real sites. Google blocked the known certificates in Chrome and had them cancelled, but people using other browsers or apps may not receive the same protection, and other organizations may also have been affected.

One Code, Five Places, One Unsubscribe Open Redirect

A credential-phishing campaign used nearly empty emails with benign PDFs that hid links to a legitimate marketing platform’s unsubscribe endpoint, which open-redirected victims to credential-harvesting pages. Each recipient received a unique code repeated across the sender name, subject, URL host, and fragment, enabling personalized targeting while SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Three mailboxes at a multinational metals and mining group received related phishing emails on 11 December 2025, each carrying a distinct per-recipient code.
  • 02The emails had effectively empty bodies and used a 93,265-byte PDF attachment named ".pdf" as the only delivery mechanism for a clickable link.
  • 03The PDF linked to a legitimate marketing platform's unsubscribe endpoint with an attacker-controlled redirect parameter that led to a landing host.
  • 04In one message, the same recipient-specific code appeared in the sender display name, subject line, twice in the landing hostname, and as the URL fragment key.
  • 05SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passed, but the messages were later quarantined and mitigated after manual review.

On 11 December 2025, three mailboxes at a multinational metals and mining group received related phishing emails over three hours and 37 minutes, each assigned a different code in the format XXXX-XXXXXX-XXXX. The emails contained no attacker-written body text or visible links, but each included a 93,265-byte PDF attachment with the filename .pdf. The PDF presented a shared-document lure and a “Review Documents” button, with two annotations pointing to the same URL.

The URL first led to a real marketing platform’s unsubscribe endpoint and used its attacker-controlled redirect parameter to send recipients to a separate landing host. In one message, the same recipient-specific code appeared in the sender display name, subject, twice in the destination hostname, and as the URL fragment key; the fragment value was the recipient’s base64-encoded mailbox address. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passed because the email was submitted through an authenticated real mailbox, while the PDF was correctly classified as clean because it only carried a link. The messages were ultimately quarantined and mitigated after manual review, highlighting the need to inspect URLs embedded in attachments and follow redirect destinations even when the first host has a legitimate reputation.

  • The campaign personalized multiple layers of each lure with the same unique code, making correlation across display names, subject lines, hostnames, and URL fragments a potentially durable detection signal even when domains are legitimate or changeable.
  • Because the malicious URL was embedded in a PDF rather than the email body, the incident’s link array was empty and the link scanner did not capture the landing page, demonstrating a visibility gap for body-focused URL inspection.
  • The attacker appears to have repurposed a genuine 2023 marketing unsubscribe URL and changed the redirect parameter, while retaining dated campaign data and nonfunctional Google-style wrapper parameters as reusable lineage artifacts for hunting.
  • The messages passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication because they were submitted through an authenticated real mailbox, showing that these checks validate sending authorization rather than whether the message content is safe.
  • The PDF was correctly classified as clean because it contained no executable or embedded malicious content; its harmful role was solely to carry a link through a legitimate service's redirect function.

Three employees at a multinational metals and mining company received emails with no message text but with a PDF attachment asking them to review a shared document. The PDF’s button first went through a real marketing company’s unsubscribe page, then sent each person to a separate fake site likely designed to collect their email login details. The messages looked trustworthy because they came through real accounts and passed normal email checks, showing that familiar services and “safe” attachments can still be used to trick people into giving away passwords.

The article describes how Aikido Security can support organizations preparing for SOC 2 audits by consolidating security findings and audit evidence in one platform. SOC 2 Type 1 assesses whether controls are appropriately designed at a particular date, while Type 2 evaluates whether those controls operated effectively over a period generally lasting three to 12 months. Type 2 therefore requires continuous, dated evidence such as logs, timestamps, and remediation histories rather than only configuration screenshots.

  • 04The article describes an evolution from smart-contract storage through transaction input data hiding to zero-value transactions that encode an active command-and-control IP address in the recipient wallet address.
  • 05The article recommends behavioral monitoring for unexpected blockchain activity, process-level inspection of developer and CI/CD systems, and automated controls to detect unauthorized build configuration and package-script changes.

Threat actors are increasingly combining open-source software supply-chain compromises with Web3-based command-and-control infrastructure to steal cloud credentials from developers and CI/CD systems. The article highlights the ChainDrop npm worm and the PolinRider campaign, which targeted packages and developer workflows to collect cloud access keys, service-account credentials, deployment secrets, and short-lived identity tokens. These techniques can provide access to cloud management consoles and APIs and may bypass multifactor authentication when other protections are absent.

Web3 command-and-control has evolved from querying fixed smart contracts for a server address, to placing encrypted instructions in blockchain transaction data, to encoding an IPv4 address in a zero-value transaction recipient address. This makes traditional domain blocking and static indicator blocklists less effective because attackers can update infrastructure through blockchain transactions without changing malicious package code. The article recommends identifying whether blockchain traffic is expected in an organization, monitoring unexpected blockchain connections from developer tools and build runners, and detecting unauthorized changes to package scripts, repository configuration, and workspace automation before builds execute.

  • For organizations that do not use blockchain services, any outbound blockchain activity can be treated as a high-confidence anomaly rather than relying only on known malicious addresses or domains.
  • ChainDrop searches the memory of running build processes, allowing it to capture short-lived cloud credentials that may never be written to disk.
  • The NullReceiver technique can encode a command-and-control IPv4 address in a zero-value blockchain transaction’s recipient address, leaving no domain, payload, smart contract, or transaction data field for filters to inspect.
  • Malicious supply-chain packages can establish persistence through project task hooks and workspace automation, causing payloads to run again when a developer opens a project or begins an AI coding session.

The article describes how attackers hide instructions for malicious software in public blockchain networks, making it harder to shut down their communications. They spread this software through widely used free programming packages, where it can run on developers’ computers and automated software-building systems to steal cloud access keys and other secrets. This affects organizations that rely on open-source code, because one compromised package can give attackers access to many companies’ online systems. The broader risk is that attackers, including North Korea-linked groups, can gain long-term access to valuable business systems while avoiding traditional website and domain blocking.

It says these agents can coordinate, adapt to obstacles in near real time, and perform work that previously required months of red-team preparation in hours. The author characterizes the publicly observed activity as noisy and closer to penetration testing than a stealthy red-team operation, particularly in the RubyGems case.

  • An assumed-breach exercise can reveal more meaningful attack paths than a perimeter scan because it begins with the possibility that an attacker already has an internal foothold.
  • The article treats AI applications that have access to company servers or data as part of the attack surface, even if their access was not deliberately approved.

The article warns that groups of AI programs can now work together to probe organizations, impersonate people, send convincing scam messages, and search for ways into computer systems much faster than human attackers. Recent public examples involving Hugging Face, DSEWiki, and RubyGems were noisy and quickly noticed, but future AI-driven attacks may be quieter and harder to spot. This matters to any organization with employee accounts, customer data, or internet-connected systems, because a tireless AI attacker can keep trying until it finds a weak point. The recommended response is to practice for incidents, protect access more carefully, and watch closely for unusual activity inside systems.

Malicious PostgreSQL Extensions in the Wild | Cyera

Cyera uncovered a Tor2Mine campaign that disguises cryptomining malware as PostgreSQL extensions for Windows and Linux, enabling code execution inside database processes. The Linux extensions evaded all tested antivirus engines and persist by modifying PostgreSQL configuration files to reload themselves.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cyera identified 20 malicious PostgreSQL extensions linked to the Tor2Mine cryptomining group: 16 for Windows and four for Linux.
  • 02The Windows extensions use an encrypted embedded payload and process hollowing to download and run an XMRigCC cryptocurrency miner.
  • 03The Linux extensions execute their payload when unloaded, copy themselves near PostgreSQL configuration files, add themselves to preload settings, and signal PostgreSQL to reload the changed configuration.
  • 04The Linux extension samples had a 0/65 VirusTotal detection rate, while their separately extracted downloader was detected by 4/66 engines.
  • 05The campaign shared command-and-control domains across Windows and Linux, and its infrastructure dates back to at least June 2018.

Cyera researchers identified 20 malicious PostgreSQL extensions linked to the Tor2Mine cryptomining group: 16 targeting Windows and four targeting Linux. The extensions use PostgreSQL’s binary-extension capability to execute code within the database process, and the campaign’s infrastructure dates back to at least 2018. Windows and Linux samples share three command-and-control domains, supporting the assessment that they are part of one cross-platform operation. The researchers reported that one campaign domain, d1.pool4883.pw, remained live during their research.

On Windows, the extension decrypts an embedded payload, uses process hollowing to run a downloader, and retrieves an XMRigCC cryptocurrency miner. On Linux, the extension activates when unloaded, extracts and runs a compressed downloader, copies itself near PostgreSQL configuration files, and adds itself to PostgreSQL preload settings for persistence. The Linux extension samples received no detections from 65 antivirus engines in VirusTotal, although the extracted downloader was detected by four of 66 engines. The same infrastructure was also linked to a separate patch.exe campaign that disabled Windows defenses and delivered the AZORult credential-stealing tool.

  • The Linux extensions execute their malicious routine when they are unloaded rather than when they are loaded, then alter PostgreSQL preload settings to arrange for themselves to be loaded again.
  • The malicious code runs inside the PostgreSQL process itself, meaning there may be no separate executable process for security tools to flag.
  • Although the embedded Linux downloader was detected by 4 of 66 antivirus engines when examined separately, the extension carrying it received no detections from 65 engines.
  • Tor2Mine’s shared infrastructure also supported a separate patch.exe campaign that disabled Windows defenses and delivered the AZORult credential-stealing tool, combining compute monetization and credential theft.
  • The PostgreSQL extensions appeared years after some of the campaign’s command-and-control domains were registered, indicating reuse of long-standing infrastructure.

Researchers found that the Tor2Mine criminal group has been hiding cryptocurrency-mining software inside add-ons for PostgreSQL, a widely used system for storing organizational data. The harmful add-ons can run inside the database program, download more software, and on Linux systems can change settings so they return after the database is restarted. Organizations that run their own PostgreSQL servers may be affected, putting valuable data systems at risk while criminals consume computing resources and may also steal credentials through related activity. The findings show that database add-ons can become a hard-to-see route into systems holding customer, employee, and other sensitive information.

CVE-2026-21589 is a critical arbitrary-file-access flaw affecting Atlassian’s self-hosted Data Center product line, including Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, Crowd, Bamboo, Crucible, and Fisheye. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read specific files within the web application root directory if they already know the exact file name and path. Those files may contain passwords, account tokens, or other digital keys that could open access to connected systems. Socket Threat Research identified a coordinated campaign of 16 malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated cryptocurrency wallet tools, including Rabby Wallet and OKX Wallet lookalikes. The extensions collected users’ 12- or 24-word recovery phrases and, in the Rabby clones, 64-character private keys during wallet import flows. They then attempted to transmit those secrets to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers. Mozilla had unpublished the extensions as of October 5.

Four larger extensions were repackaged Rabby applications branded as “Raabby WaIIet,” with secret-stealing hooks inserted into wallet import functions and user-interface paths. Twelve smaller extensions used an OKX-like “Portal WALLET” interface that prompted users for recovery phrases; one was broken because its background script was not loaded and did not handle the frontend’s message type. Fifteen extensions used related Workers infrastructure and shared the EQOx7EIPZSNi campaign marker, while all declared no Firefox data collection despite transmitting wallet recovery material. Anyone who entered a real recovery phrase or private key is advised to create a new wallet from a clean device, transfer assets immediately, and treat all accounts derived from the exposed recovery phrase as compromised.

  • The Rabby-clone extensions inserted secret-stealing calls directly into legitimate wallet import functions and also into user-interface import paths, so a single entered secret could trigger multiple outbound transmissions.
  • The Rabby-clone family sent secrets in GET URL parameters, which can expose them not only to the receiving Worker but also to request logs and any intermediary that records URLs.
  • One compact extension claimed in comments that it sent only a hash and word count, but its code explicitly placed the full recovery phrase in the outbound `w` field, providing direct evidence that the comments concealed its actual behavior.
  • The nonfunctional `sipoo-grozza` package still contained recovery-phrase collection code and three methods for sending the phrase away; its failure resulted from packaging and message-routing mistakes rather than the absence of theft functionality.
  • The campaign varied extension names, versions, IDs, and descriptions while reusing identical payload files, a shared campaign marker, and related Cloudflare Worker infrastructure, enabling defenders to hunt for related packages using shared code hashes and markers.

Researchers found 16 Firefox add-ons that pretended to be cryptocurrency wallet tools, including lookalikes of Rabby and OKX Wallet. When people typed in their wallet recovery words or private keys, the add-ons sent those secrets to criminals, who could use them to take control of the affected wallets and steal funds. Mozilla has removed the add-ons, but anyone who used one and entered real wallet details should create a new wallet on a clean device and move their assets right away, because changing an add-on password does not make a stolen recovery phrase safe.

  • The exposed administrative platform shows an agent-and-reseller business model with commission rates, device quotas, and a 75-account roster, indicating that the kit is operated as a commercial service rather than solely by a single intrusion team.
  • The production delivery system uses five hash-distinct variant sets, short-lived IP-bound download tokens, prior-visit checks, and iOS-style user-agent checks, making leaked payload links unusable within minutes and reducing reliance on fixed file hashes for detection.
  • Twenty-two wallet-module samples found in the wild use the separate 66ds[.]lol C2 and differ from the production code primarily by replacing the fallback C2 string, showing that a separate operator reused the same core kit without modifying its broader framework.
  • The gooll kernel stage does not rely on preloaded device-specific memory-address tables; it fingerprints the phone at runtime and uses multiple fallback paths, which the article identifies as a design difference from older DarkSword chains.

Researchers found publicly accessible server folders that exposed a criminal service built to break into iPhones and steal cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases, account details, and other phone data. The service appears to be run by a Chinese-speaking group that sells access to other operators, and evidence shows real iPhone users in China and Hong Kong repeatedly connecting to its malicious web pages. This matters because someone who gets a wallet recovery phrase can take control of the victim’s cryptocurrency, while the group is also preparing new ways to target future iPhone software versions.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a detailed report on live DarkSword/Coruna infrastructure supporting active iOS exploitation and cryptocurrency-wallet theft, including observed victim beaconing, C2 platforms, payloads, and actionable infrastructure indicators. It also documents an unfinished iOS 26 exploit-development lead and a separate operator using the same kit in the wild.

Optional · 55 announcement 07 Oct 2026 16:30 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Building an evidence-grounded agentic security operations harness on Cloudflare

Cloudflare has launched an evidence-grounded, multi-agent AI security-operations harness in Managed Defense that deterministically gathers and validates alert evidence before using specialist models to recommend analyst-reviewed dispositions and mitigations. The system is designed to reduce alert noise and hallucinations while preserving tenant boundaries, auditability, and explicit handling of missing data.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cloudflare’s Managed Defense harness uses deterministic reconnaissance workflows to collect versioned evidence on customer identity, detection history, traffic baselines, enforcement outcomes, and network observations before model analysis begins.
  • 02Cloudflare uses Clef on Workers AI to triage alerts, with high-likelihood false positives skipping specialist AI-agent analysis and known high-volume noise classified as passive.
  • 03For alerts requiring deeper review, a coordinator runs traffic analysis, customer context, global telemetry, and threat-intelligence specialists in parallel, followed by a synthesis agent that cannot retrieve new evidence or use classifications outside an approved vocabulary.
  • 04The system creates a versioned evidence package and validates that specialist findings cite evidence belonging to the investigation; it records coverage gaps when sources fail or data is unavailable.
  • 05Managed Defense Analysts retain responsibility for final decisions and mitigations, while the advisory can recommend actions such as rate-limiting rules, WAF custom rules, or DDoS-protection changes.

Cloudflare has introduced a multi-agent AI security-operations harness for eligible application-security alerts and cases in Cloudflare Managed Defense. The system is intended to help Managed Defense Analysts handle large volumes of alerts by assembling evidence, connecting related detections, identifying gaps, and recommending next steps. Analysts remain responsible for the final decision and any mitigation.

Before AI analysis, deterministic reconnaissance workflows collect a versioned snapshot of customer identity, detection history, traffic baselines, enforcement outcomes, and network observations. Clef, Cloudflare’s open-source decision model running on Workers AI, filters likely false positives and later evaluates whether the available evidence is sufficient and non-contradictory for a decision. Specialist agents review traffic, customer history, privacy-preserving global telemetry, and admitted threat-intelligence indicators, while application code validates citations, enforces customer scope, and records unavailable or incomplete evidence rather than treating it as a negative result.

  • Cloudflare found that giving one general-purpose AI agent the entire investigation caused unsupported claims because detections, telemetry, policies, and threat intelligence were treated as if they had the same evidentiary authority.
  • By collecting a fixed reconnaissance snapshot before AI analysis, Cloudflare can replay the same investigation and attribute differences in results to interpretation rather than changing retrieved data.
  • The system treats “not checked,” “checked with no match,” and “checked with evidence supporting absence” as different states, preventing a failed or incomplete lookup from being presented as a negative result.
  • The global-telemetry component can assess Internet-wide patterns using aggregates without receiving another customer’s individual records or identity.
  • When evidence is insufficient, the system does not provide an attack classification or disposition recommendation, even though it may still describe what is unusual for that customer.

Cloudflare has introduced a system for its Managed Defense service that uses several AI helpers to sort through large numbers of security warnings and gather the facts behind them. It is meant to help Cloudflare’s security analysts decide faster which warnings are harmless, which may need action, and what protective changes could help. This matters to organizations using Cloudflare because too many warnings can overwhelm people and cause real threats to be missed, while the system keeps a human responsible for the final decision.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a product announcement and architecture overview for Cloudflare Managed Defense’s AI alert-analysis harness, not a report of an active threat, breach, or urgent vulnerability. It offers useful operational design details on evidence validation, scope enforcement, and handling incomplete data, but remains a vendor-specific, low-urgency development.

UK Cybercrime Journal: Police Cryptocurrency Crime Operations in 2026

UK law enforcement actions in 2026 show cryptocurrency crime increasingly combines police-impersonation and seed-phrase scams with physical coercion, while unregistered P2P exchanges enable laundering. Crypto holders should protect recovery phrases, independently verify urgent calls, limit public exposure of holdings, and use multisig or time-locked custody to reduce forced-transfer risk.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Three Sheffield teenagers posing as Amazon delivery drivers used violence during a London home invasion and forced a victim to transfer £3.1 million in cryptocurrency.
  • 02A multi-force UK operation arrested and charged ten suspects accused of calling victims while posing as police officers or cryptocurrency-platform representatives to obtain wallet recovery phrases.
  • 03Three men were jailed for defrauding eight victims of more than £4 million in cryptocurrency by impersonating police and directing funds to purported secure police accounts.
  • 04The FCA, HMRC, and Metropolitan Police targeted three London premises alleged to be operating unregistered peer-to-peer cryptocurrency exchanges outside anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing requirements.
  • 05The article advises cryptocurrency holders never to disclose recovery phrases, independently verify unexpected police or exchange calls, and consider multi-signature and time-locked storage.

UK enforcement actions in 2026 addressed cryptocurrency crime ranging from a violent London home invasion to phone-based fraud and unregistered peer-to-peer trading operations. In one case, three Sheffield teenagers posing as Amazon delivery drivers forced a victim to transfer £3.1 million in cryptocurrency; police detained them within hours and the assets were recovered within 72 hours. Separate multi-force operations arrested alleged fraudsters who posed as police officers or cryptocurrency-platform representatives to obtain wallet recovery phrases, while another group was jailed after stealing more than £4 million from eight victims.

The cases show how criminals combine social engineering with physical coercion, using trusted police branding to make victims reveal recovery phrases or move money to supposed safe accounts. The FCA, HMRC, and Metropolitan Police also targeted three London premises alleged to be operating unregistered peer-to-peer cryptocurrency exchanges outside required anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing controls. The article advises holders to avoid public disclosure of holdings and locations, never share recovery phrases, verify unexpected calls through official numbers, and consider multi-signature wallets or time-locked storage to limit forced transfers.

  • Police impersonation can defeat ordinary account protections because victims may be pressured into voluntarily revealing wallet recovery phrases or approving transfers.
  • Public social-media posts about wealth, holdings, or location can make cryptocurrency owners easier to identify and target for in-person robbery.
  • Multi-signature wallets and time-locked storage can reduce the immediate ability of criminals to force a cryptocurrency transfer during a physical home invasion.
  • Unregistered peer-to-peer cryptocurrency businesses can provide a route for illicit digital funds to be converted into cash or apparently legitimate bank transfers.
  • The Sheffield suspects' Snapchat posts illustrate that criminals’ public online activity can create an investigative opportunity for law enforcement.

In 2026, UK authorities acted against several cryptocurrency crimes, including a violent home robbery, phone scams where criminals pretended to be police or crypto companies, and unregistered businesses used to turn digital funds into cash. People with cryptocurrency, especially those who publicly display their wealth, can be targeted and pressured or tricked into giving away the secret recovery words that control their money. The cases show that digital theft can lead to real-world harm and that criminals may use poorly regulated trading channels to hide or spend stolen funds.

Optional · 52 news 07 Oct 2026 14:01 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Health-ISAC Urges Validation of Restored Clinical Systems After June Cyber Exercise

Health-ISAC’s after-action report from its June 2026 tabletop exercise urges health systems to predefine procedures for validating that restored clinical systems are safe and reliable before returning them to use after a cyber incident.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Health-ISAC published an after-action report on October 5, 2026, recommending that health systems define how they will validate restored clinical systems before the next cyber incident.
  • 02The 2026 Americas Hobby Exercise was an all-day workshop and tabletop exercise held on June 24.
  • 03The exercise included health systems, medical technology and pharmaceutical companies, Water-ISAC and water-sector representatives, and government partners.
  • 04Its fictional scenario combined drought, wildfires, brownouts, falling water pressure, electronic health-record logouts, nurse-call delays, and drug shortages.
  • 05The report summarizes discussion themes and recommendations but does not measure participants’ response or recovery performance.

Health-ISAC published an after-action report on October 5, 2026, for its 2026 Americas Hobby Exercise, an all-day workshop and tabletop exercise held June 24. The organization recommends that health systems define in advance how they will validate restored clinical systems before another cyber incident. Health-ISAC emphasizes that bringing a system back online does not by itself show that clinicians can safely rely on it.

The exercise included health systems, medical technology and pharmaceutical companies, Water-ISAC, water-sector representatives, and government partners. Its fictional scenario combined drought, wildfires, brownouts, and falling water pressure with electronic health-record logouts, nurse-call delays, and drug shortages. Participants were deliberately left unsure whether the disruptions resulted from a cyberattack, a natural disaster, or both, while the report summarizes discussion themes and recommendations rather than measuring response or recovery performance.

  • The exercise deliberately made it unclear whether disruptions were caused by a cyberattack, a natural disaster, or both, highlighting that health organizations may need to respond before the cause is known.
  • Health-ISAC’s central recommendation is not merely to restore clinical systems, but to establish in advance how clinicians will confirm those systems can be safely relied upon.
  • The scenario linked clinical disruptions such as electronic health-record logouts and nurse-call delays with infrastructure stresses including drought, wildfires, power problems, and falling water pressure.
  • The report is intended to capture discussion themes and recommendations rather than assess how well participants performed during response and recovery.

Health-ISAC says hospitals and other health organizations should plan how they will confirm that patient-care computer systems work safely after they have been restored following a cyber incident. Its June exercise brought together health, medical technology, drug, water-sector, and government participants to consider a situation involving drought, wildfires, power problems, low water pressure, medical-record logouts, delayed nurse calls, and medicine shortages. The exercise showed that disruptions can have unclear causes and that simply turning systems back on may not mean clinicians can safely depend on them, creating potential risks for patient care.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

The article reports on a specific Health-ISAC tabletop exercise and its after-action recommendations, but it does not disclose an active incident, vulnerability, or urgent threat. Its main value is as a best-practice reminder for healthcare organizations to validate clinical systems after restoration.

breach notifications concept

breached concept

capture concept

china

A threat-actor group described in security reporting as Chinese-speaking.

CISOs are senior leaders responsible for an organization’s information security.

civilian concept

classification concept

Classified information is government information restricted because releasing it could harm national security or other protected interests.
claude

Claude is a family of artificial-intelligence language models made by Anthropic.
Claude Mythos 5.1 product
An AI model product referenced in security testing and evaluation.

An Anthropic artificial-intelligence model designed to generate and analyze text.

An Anthropic AI language model designed to understand and generate text.

Clinical systems are healthcare technologies used to support patient care, records, scheduling, testing, or treatment.
cloud concept

cloud services concept

CloudSEK is a cybersecurity company that monitors online threats, leaked data, and criminal activity on the internet.
cluster concept
A group of connected computers or appliances that work together as one system.
co-conspirators threat-actor

code execution technique
Code execution means an attacker can make a computer or server run commands or software of their choosing.
coding concept
Coding is writing instructions in a programming language so a computer can perform tasks.
Coercion concept
Coercion is forcing or pressuring someone to do something against their will, sometimes used in scams or extortion.
Collaboration Tools concept
Collaboration tools are apps that let people communicate, share files, and work together.

Command and control domains are internet addresses malware uses to receive instructions from its operators.
command execution technique
